exp.0:0:
Jude presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ, that is, someone who belongs to Him and obeys Him. He says he is the brother of James. He writes to those who are called, the ones God invited to follow Him. He also calls them sanctified, meaning set apart for God, and preserved, meaning cared for and kept safe by Jesus Christ.

The writer is Jude, a Christian leader. Many believe he was the brother of Jesus, since James is named as His brother, although the letter does not state this in so many words. What we do see in the verses that follow is his purpose: he wanted to write about the salvation we all share, but he saw the need to encourage believers to defend the faith they received with firmness.

For today: if you belong to Christ, your security does not rest on your own strength, but on the fact that He keeps you. Live with humility and confidence, and pray that He will hold you steady.
exp.0:3:
What it says: Jude warns that some people have slipped in quietly among believers, without anyone noticing. They are called ungodly, meaning they do not honor God. They use grace as an excuse to live without restraint, a disordered and immoral way of life, and they reject God and Jesus Christ as Lord. The phrase about being marked out long ago for this judgment is understood in several ways: some see a condemnation announced beforehand in the Scriptures, others see a judgment already determined for those who live this way.

Context: Jude, who presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes to believers. He wanted to speak to them about salvation, but he felt more urgency to call them to defend the faith, because there were false teachers within the communities.

For today: God's grace forgives us, but it also transforms us. Examine whether you use grace as permission to sin, and ask Jesus to be truly your Lord.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that Sodom, Gomorrah and the nearby cities fell into sexual immorality and went after "strange flesh," that is, desires and practices contrary to the natural order God established. For this reason God judged them, and their destruction stands as an example for everyone.

Sexual immorality means having sexual relations outside the plan of God. Eternal fire speaks of a judgment with lasting consequences.

Jude, who presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes to warn believers about false teachers who had infiltrated the church. He gives three examples from the past: unbelieving Israel, the fallen angels, and Sodom. In each case, God judged those who rebelled.

For today: do not take God's grace lightly. Examine your life honestly, ask forgiveness where needed, and seek to live in purity, trusting that Christ gives strength to change.
exp.0:9:
Jude says that these people speak evil, with contempt, of spiritual things they do not understand. And in the things they do know by instinct, such as bodily desires, they destroy themselves, just like animals that do not reason. Animals with no reason, that only follow their urges, is what the phrase means.

Jude is writing to believers to warn them against false teachers who had slipped into the church. He has just mentioned that not even the archangel Michael dared to insult the devil, but left the judgment in God's hands. The false teachers, by contrast, mock with pride. The details of that scene involving Michael are interpreted in several ways.

For today: before criticizing or mocking what we do not understand, let us practice humility. Let us ask questions, study the Bible, and leave the final judgment to God.
exp.0:10:
Jude says "Woe to them!" as a serious warning, much like the warnings the prophets gave. He mentions three figures from the Old Testament: Cain, who killed his brother out of envy and pride; Balaam, who let himself be carried away by the desire to make money; and Korah, who rebelled against the leadership of Moses. "Rebellion" means defiance or opposition, and "perished" indicates that they came to a bad end.

Jude writes to believers to alert them to false teachers who had slipped into the churches. He compares them to these three examples: pride and violence, love of money, and rebellion against the authority God had placed. What follows in the text describes how these men live.

For today: examine your motives when you teach, serve, or lead. Ask God to free you from envy, from the love of money, and from pride that will not accept correction.
exp.0:11:
The explanation says that certain people within the church are like spots or hidden rocks at the love feasts, that is, the shared meals of the believers. They eat without reverence, thinking only of themselves. To feed themselves, in place of caring for the flock, means looking after and nourishing only their own interests. They are like clouds without water, which promise rain but do not give it, and like autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, that is, completely dry and uprooted.

Jude, the brother of James, writes to the believers to warn them about false teachers who had slipped into the community. He uses strong images from nature to show that their religious appearance has no real fruit.

Some translators understand the word rendered as spots as hidden rocks; the Greek word allows both meanings.

For today: do not be impressed only by pretty words or by a good image. Look at the fruit: humility, love and service to others. And examine your own heart so that your faith bears fruit and not only appearance.
exp.0:17:
Jude reminds his readers that the apostles had already warned them of something. In the last times there would be mockers, that is, people who ridicule what is sacred and scoff at the faith. Their way of living would not be guided by God, but by their own evil desires.

Jude writes to beloved believers to encourage them to defend the faith. He has just described certain people who had slipped in among them: grumblers, proud people, and those interested only in their own gain. He tells them not to be surprised, because the apostles had already foreseen this. Scholars understand the phrase "the last time" in different ways, but all agree that Jude is speaking of a present reality.

When someone mocks your faith, do not lose heart: God had already warned of it. Stand firm, pray, and keep growing in Christ without letting those mockeries carry you away.
exp.0:20:
The explanation says that believers should hold firmly within the love of God, that is, keep living in his care and closeness. Meanwhile, they wait with confidence for Jesus Christ, through his mercy, to give them eternal life. Keeping yourselves in the love of God means staying in it. Waiting here is a confident expectation, not a doubtful one.

Jude, who presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes to warn against false teachers who were dividing the church. In opposition to them, he encourages his beloved readers to grow in faith, pray in the Spirit, and remain in the love of God. Then he asks them to help with compassion those who doubt or wander away.

For today: take care of your spiritual life with simple habits, such as praying, reading the Bible, and being with other believers. In this way you remain in the love of God, trusting in his mercy and not in your own strength.
exp.0:22:
It says that we should help save other people by rescuing them urgently, like someone pulling a person out of a fire. We do this with fear, meaning with seriousness and care, knowing how dangerous sin is. Helping others to be saved means helping them come to salvation. To reject something is to turn away from it in strong disgust; the garment stained by sin is an image of everything that sin has defiled.

Jude, brother of James, writes to believers who were in danger from false teachers who twisted the grace of God. Earlier he asked them to remain in the love of God and to have compassion on those who doubt. Scholars explain in various ways how the groups of people in these verses are divided, but the central idea is clear: love with firmness.

For today: if someone close to you moves away from God, do not ignore them or judge them from a distance. Pray for that person and speak to them with love and truth, taking care not to be drawn into the same path.
exp.0:14:
This verse says that the Lord comes to carry out judgment on everyone. He will expose to the ungodly their guilt for every wicked act they committed without regard for God, and for the harsh words they spoke against him. Here "to convict" means to bring out into the open and prove their guilt. The ungodly are those who live without fear or reverence for God.

Jude writes to believers to warn them against false teachers who had slipped into the church. To show that God judges evil, he quotes a prophecy from Enoch. That prophecy does not appear in the Old Testament, but in an ancient Jewish book called 1 Enoch, and scholars debate how this quotation should be understood.

God sees everything, even our words, and one day he will bring it all into the light. This invites us to speak with respect, to live with humility, and to trust that God will do justice.
exp.0:19:
The explanation says that the believers, whom Jude calls "beloved," must keep growing in their faith. The phrase "building yourselves up" means to build little by little, like a house. "Most holy faith" refers to the truths of the gospel that God gave us. "Praying in the Holy Spirit" is usually understood as praying guided by the Spirit, in communion with Him. "But" is the word that introduces the contrast here.

Jude, who presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes to believers threatened by false teachers and scoffers. These people caused divisions and lived according to their desires. Against them, Jude does not only tell them to flee, but gives them a positive path: to strengthen themselves in the faith, to pray, and to remain in the love of God.

For today: it is not enough to reject what is wrong; we must also care for what is good. Set aside time each day to read the Bible and pray, asking the Spirit to guide you and keep you firm.
exp.0:12:
They are like wild waves of the sea, which throw up foam, and the foam is their own shame and sins. They are also like wandering stars, which leave their course, and for them the blackest darkness has been kept forever. "Wild" means fierce or out of control; "foaming up" means throwing up foam; "wandering" means being lost; "forever" means for all time.

Jude, the brother of James, writes to believers to warn them against false teachers who had slipped into the churches. They lived without fear of God, looked out for their own gain, and misled others. Jude uses images from nature to show that their appearance is impressive, but they have no direction and no true light. He announces that God will judge them.

Today, do not let yourself be carried away by someone who speaks with force but lives without direction. Always compare what you hear with the Bible, and follow Christ, the true light.
exp.0:13:
This verse says that Enoch, the seventh man after Adam, announced a message from God about the false teachers Jude describes. Enoch said that the Lord is coming with myriads of his holy ones.

"The Lord is coming" speaks of something so certain that it is spoken of as though it were already underway. "Myriads" refers to the vast multitudes of holy beings who come with him.

Jude is the writer, and he warns believers against people who had slipped into the church and lived without fear of God. To strengthen his warning, he quotes a prophecy of Enoch. That quotation does not appear in the Old Testament but in the apocryphal book of Enoch, which Jewish tradition knew. Scholars discuss how this should be understood, but Jude uses it because his message is true.

For today: God sees all injustice, and one day he will judge it. We can live with reverence and hope, without envying those who live wickedly.
exp.0:1:
He says that Jude wishes God would give them plenty of three things: mercy, peace, and love. The words "be multiplied" mean that these things should increase and grow more and more in the lives of believers. It is not a simple greeting; it is a prayer for them. Mercy is God's compassion toward us, peace is the calm that comes from being right with Him, and love is God's care that is also reflected among brothers and sisters.

The one speaking is Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James. He writes to believers who have been called and kept by God. Shortly afterward he warns them that they must defend the faith, because some people had slipped in unnoticed and were twisting God's grace to justify a life without restraint. Before correcting them, Jude first blesses them.

For today: when you have to correct or warn someone, do it with truth, but also with love. Pray that God would multiply His mercy, His peace, and His love to them.
exp.0:23:
This verse says that God is able to keep us from stumbling and to present us unblemished in his glorious presence, filled with great joy. The word "keep" means to care for and protect. "Unblemished" means without any flaw or stain that could be held against us.

Jude, who presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes to believers who were threatened by false teachers who twisted the grace of God. After warning them very seriously and asking them to help others who doubt or are being lost, he closes with this praise. He reminds them that their steadfastness does not depend on them alone, but on God.

For today: when you feel that your faith is weak or that you might fail, remain responsible, but rest in the fact that God sustains you. Pray asking for his help every day and trust in his faithfulness.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that certain angels did not stay within the domain God had given them but abandoned their proper dwelling. Because of this, God has kept them in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day.

Jude, the brother of James, writes to warn believers about false teachers who had slipped into the church and were using grace as an excuse to live badly. He gives three examples of judgment: unbelieving Israel, these angels, and Sodom. Some think he is referring to a known Jewish tradition; others, to an angelic rebellion. Not everyone agrees.

For today: God gives us a place and a responsibility. Let us keep humility and obedience, without abusing his grace.
exp.0:16:
Jude calls his readers "beloved" and asks them to remember what was foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. "Remember" means "keep in mind." "But" marks the contrast. After describing the false teachers, Jude turns to what gives believers stability.

The writer is Jude, who presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James. He writes because some people in the churches were grumbling, following their own desires, and seeking their own advantage. He reminds them that this should not take them by surprise, since the apostles had already spoken about it beforehand.

For today: when voices arise that confuse or divide, return to the apostolic teaching in the Bible. Read it regularly, so that your faith does not depend on trends or opinions, but on what Christ taught through his apostles.
exp.0:18:
This verse describes the scoffers the previous verse spoke of. It says they cause divisions among believers. "Worldly" means they live guided by their natural instincts and desires, not by God. And "devoid of the Spirit" means they do not have the Holy Spirit in their lives.

Jude, who presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes to believers who were facing false teachers who had slipped into the church. He reminds them of what the apostles had already warned: in the last times there would be scoffers. Then, in verse 20, he encourages them to build themselves up in the faith and pray in the Holy Spirit.

For today: instead of fueling quarrels or gossip in the church, seek the guidance of the Holy Spirit through prayer and the Word, and pursue unity with your brothers and sisters. In this way, you guard your own faith and that of others.
exp.0:2:
Jude calls his readers "beloved." He says he had wanted to write to them about the salvation that all believers share, but he found that he had to change his subject and urge them to contend earnestly, that is, to struggle firmly, for the faith that was entrusted once for all to the saints, the believers.

Jude, who presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, writes to Christians who were in danger. According to the verses that follow, certain people had slipped in who twisted God's grace to justify a disorderly life. The Bible does not say precisely which churches he was addressing.

Today, loving the Christian faith includes knowing it and caring for it. We can read the Bible regularly and, with humility and respect, refuse to accept teachings that contradict what Christ and the apostles left us.
exp.0:4:
Jude says he wants to remind them of something they already know. To "remind" here means to bring something back to mind with seriousness. Jesus delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, but afterward He destroyed those who did not believe. In the wilderness, many of that generation died because of their unbelief.

Jude, who presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ, writes to believers worried about false teachers who had slipped in among them. They were using grace as an excuse to live without restraint. Jude uses the example of Israel to show that having been rescued does not guarantee anything if one later abandons the faith.

For today: do not take God's grace lightly. If He has saved you, respond with trust and obedience, and check whether there is any area where you are doubting or living as if it did not matter.
exp.0:24:
It says that glory, majesty, dominion and authority belong to the only God our Savior, and that this is through Jesus Christ our Lord. The majesty here means his greatness and splendor, the dominion means his rule as King, and the authority means his right to act and to be obeyed. This is so before all time, now, and for all eternity. The word "Amen" means "so be it."

Jude, who presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes this letter to warn against false teachers who had slipped in among the believers. After urging readers to take care of themselves and to help others, he ends with this praise. He trusts that God is the one who keeps his own from falling and presents them before his glory with joy.

For today: when you feel weak or surrounded by confusion, remember that your perseverance does not depend only on your own strength. End your day by praising God, who is able to sustain and guide you with wisdom.
exp.0:21:
Jude 1:22 tells us to show mercy to those who doubt or waver in their faith. The Berean Standard Bible wording, "have mercy on those who doubt," makes clear that the call is to tenderness toward people who are hesitating. Mercy here means showing kindness and gentleness toward those who are unsure. The Greek text has some variant readings, but the central idea is the same: treat with gentleness the person who is wavering.

Jude, who presents himself as a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, writes to believers threatened by false teachers who twisted God's grace. After warning them firmly, he urges them to remain steadfast in the love of God. Then he shows them how to treat others: with mercy toward those who doubt, and with urgency toward those who are in serious danger.

For today: if you know someone who doubts their faith, do not judge or scold them. Listen to them with patience, pray for them, and respond with love and wisdom, according to what they need.
exp.0:7:
He says that certain people who have slipped into the church, whom he calls "dreamers," do the same as the earlier examples. "Defile their bodies" means that they corrupt themselves through immoral conduct. "Reject authority" means that they scorn those in charge, and "slander glorious beings" means that they speak ill of beings who hold honor. Some think this refers to angels; others, to any legitimate authority.

Jude, brother of James, writes to believers to warn them against false teachers who had crept in among them. He reminds them of past punishments, such as that of Sodom and of the fallen angels, to show that God does not overlook rebellion or impurity.

Today we can examine our lives with humility. If a message excuses what is impure or teaches people to reject all authority, it is wise to compare it with the Bible. And let us ourselves strive to live with purity and respect.
exp.0:8:
It says that the archangel Michael, though he is a very powerful being, argued with the devil about the body of Moses and did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him on his own authority. He only said: "The Lord rebuke you!"

The phrase "argued" in the verse means the same as "disputed" in the explanation, and "slanderous charge" is an accusation made with insults.

Jude writes to believers to warn them against false teachers who mocked spiritual authorities. His point is that even Michael did not place himself in God's place as judge. This story does not appear in the Old Testament; some think Jude drew on an ancient Jewish tradition, and its exact origin is not known for certain.

For today: when we face evil or injustice, let us not act with pride or with hurtful words. Let us ask God to correct and judge, and keep humility and respect.
exp.0:15:
These men are grumblers and discontented complainers, following after their own lusts. They speak with arrogance, and they flatter others for their own advantage. In this verse, the first two traits describe people who are always unhappy and quick to find fault, while the last two describe people who puff others up with empty praise only when it benefits them.

Jude writes to warn believers about false teachers who had slipped into the church. He has just quoted Enoch, a prophecy about God coming to judge the ungodly, and he reminds his readers that the apostles had already warned them about these mockers.

For today: examine your words. Do you complain easily, or flatter people to get something? Ask God for a grateful and sincere heart.

sum.0: Jude writes to believers to urge them to stand firmly for the faith, because ungodly people have crept in among them who twist God's grace and live without restraint. He reminds them of past judgments on Israel, on the angels, and on Sodom, and encourages them to remain in God's love, to pray, to help those who doubt, and to trust that God is able to keep them.
